rulings.reasoning: The direction of the concession is right: on the naive sigma^2/8 test the keeper does not clear LVR on any window (my recomputation: 7d fees $1,847 vs LVR $7.5-9.1k at 50-55% sigma, ratio 0.20-0.25; 24h realised 9.4 bps vs 11.6 bps break-even). But the rebuttal mislabels its number: the 1.55% vs 3.81% figure is DATA-PACK section 5 with no stated window; the 7d figure from res.json is 0.73% and 48h is 2.11%. More important for the wording: the naive test is an upper bound that ignores the fee band and block time. ETH hourly sigma is ~59 bps; a 9-23 bps fee is a wide no-trade band on a sub-second chain, so realised arb loss is likely a fraction of sigma^2/8 (this is exactly the arXiv 2404.05803 mechanism R cites). So 'has not been shown to clear LVR' should read 'cannot be assessed on the naive test; realised loss is bounded above by it and markouts are the only measurement'.

rulings.reasoning: The conclusion (do not wait) survives; the mechanism does not. Points 'follow the swap fees your liquidity actually earns', so an LP washing its own pool pays f*(1-s) per dollar and earns points proportional to f*s: both scale with f and the wash economics are invariant to the fee level. What is true for LPs is different: wash is non-toxic volume, so its fees offset LVR while it lasts, which makes the surge-window break-evens honestly lower; but it ends 5 October, so pricing to the 48h numbers is wrong and pricing to the 7d numbers (the higher ones) is right. That supports moving now on SPY and NVDA. Wash also makes C7's total-share metric unreliable, which is a second reason to define the trigger on routed dollars. Labelling the contract senders is worth doing and is not a gate.

rulings.reasoning: The premise is right: per-tier break-even in pips folds in this week's volume mix and the variance ratios come from 730 days of bars. But the rule as stated ('break-even sets the open tier's level only') is wrong for LPs and V2 itself does not follow it. LP P&L is additive across tiers, so a tier under its own break-even loses money regardless of how pretty the shape is. V2's SPY overnight is 0.47x open against a 0.26 variance ratio, NVDA 0.75x against 0.48, META 0.78x against 0.44, and the NVDA/SPY suggestion is 1.0x against 0.66; only GLD follows the variance shape. In every one of those cases V2 picked the higher, break-even-based number, and for NVDA that choice is what carries LP P&L (the overnight tier holds 70% of NVDA's weekly volume; at the variance-shape 480 it would sit under its 630 pip 7d break-even). The defensible rule is: each tier at or above its own break-even with margin, and the variance shape as the prior where a tier's volume is too thin to measure (closed tiers, dust pools).

rulings.reasoning: The mismatch is real: SessionLib.classify returns CLOSED from Friday 16:00 ET through Sunday, MAX_SESSION_LENGTH is 12h, the baked table is NYSE. With a flat 1500/1500 weekday that puts the whole of Sunday at 1500, which captures the Sunday 18:00 ET reopen (the only non-zero variance in the CLOSED tier, 1.77x OPEN per hour) at the cost of over-pricing Sunday 00:00-18:00 when nothing trades against a reference. setDayOverrides takes a monthly bitmap and the closure cap does not count force-opens, so it is four or five bits a month. NYSE holidays COMEX trades on are the same mechanism. Only the daily 17:00-18:00 break and a session longer than 12h need bytecode. So: accept the finding, change the action to 'Sunday FORCE_OPEN overrides now, contracts change later'.

The 'argues for the raise' half is weaker than stated. Points follow fees earned pro rata, so a washer's points share is roughly W s / (V + W), independent of the fee, while the cost per dollar washed is f (1 - s). Raising f does raise the cost, but only in proportion to (1 - s): for a dominant concentrated LP washing through its own range the cost is near zero at any fee, and a higher fee makes each washed dollar worth more in points-eligible fees. So the raise deters small-share washers and does nothing to a dominant one. The bigger consequence of wash, which the rebuttal skips, is that it inflates the per-tier volume in every break-even, so the break-evens are understated and the case for raising is stronger, not weaker. Labelling the senders therefore changes the level, even if not the direction.
